nodes.title: Western Nebraska family (family D) with autosomal dominant parkinsonism.

nodes.label: Wszolek et al. (1995) described a large family (family D) from western Nebraska, whose ancestors probably immigrated to the United States from England, with 188 individuals spanning 6 generations and 18 affected members. Affected members developed typical levodopa-responsive Parkinson disease with bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and impaired postural reflexes; eye movement abnormalities, pyramidal and cerebellar signs, sensory disturbances, and orthostatic blood pressure changes did not occur. Disease progression was slow.
Parkinsonism with favorable response to dopaminergic medication
Wszolek et al. (1995) found that parkinsonism in family D was inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

Wszolek et al. (1995) reported that PET with [18F]-6-fluoro-L-dopa in an affected member of family D showed decreased fluorodopa uptake in a pattern consistent with Parkinson disease, and autopsy of another affected member showed neuronal and pigmentary loss, gliosis, and Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra pars compacta. The authors concluded that the disorder closely resembled, if not identical to, idiopathic PD.

Hasegawa and Kowa (1997) reported a family from Sagamihara City (Japan) with Parkinson disease across 5 generations. The clinical features did not differ from those of common Parkinson disease, and the title notes older age at onset and a good response to levodopa therapy.
Hasegawa and Kowa (1997) reported that Parkinson disease was inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern through 5 generations of the Sagamihara family.

In autopsied members of the Sagamihara family, Hasegawa and Kowa (1997) found neuropathology that differed from typical Parkinson disease. Loss of melanin-containing cells was mild to moderate, and the number of locus ceruleus neurons was maintained. No Lewy bodies were found in any region where Lewy bodies frequently appear in Parkinson disease.
Neuronal loss in central nervous system

Funayama et al. (2002) performed genomewide linkage analysis in a Japanese family with autosomal dominant parkinsonism. Parametric two-point analysis gave a maximum lod score of 4.32 at D12S345 (12p11.21), and multipoint analysis gave a maximum lod score of 4.71 at D12S85 (12q12). Haplotype analysis found obligate recombinations at D12S1631 and D12S339, which defined a 13.6-cM disease-associated interval in 12p11.2-q13.1. Nonparametric two-point and multipoint analyses gave maximum lod scores of 14.2 and 24.9 at D12S345.
Funayama et al. (2002) described a Japanese family with autosomal dominant parkinsonism whose clinical features were compatible with those of common Parkinson disease.

Funayama et al. (2002) found that all patients in the family shared the disease-associated haplotype, but some unaffected individuals also carried it. They suggested that penetrance in this family was incomplete and that environmental or other genetic factors modify expression of the disease.
Funayama et al. (2002) noted that this chromosome 12 region differs from every known locus for hereditary parkinsonism.
Funayama et al. (2002) named the new parkinsonism locus on chromosome 12p11.2-q13.1 PARK8.

Zimprich et al. (2004) tested 21 white families with Parkinson disease and a pattern compatible with autosomal dominant transmission (at least 3 affected individuals in more than 1 generation) for linkage to the PARK8 region on centromeric chromosome 12, using 29 markers. In total they tested 167 family members (84 affected, 83 unaffected). Assuming heterogeneity and using an affecteds-only model, they obtained a maximum multipoint lod score of 2.01 (P = 0.0047) in the whole sample, with an estimated 0.32 proportion of linked families.

Zimprich et al. (2004) found that 2 families, family A (German Canadian) and family D (from western Nebraska), each showed significant linkage to PARK8. Their combined maximum multipoint lod score was 3.33 under an affecteds-only model and 3.92 under a penetrance-dependent model. The 1-lod support interval placed the disease locus between a CA repeat on genomic clone AC025253 (44.5 Mb) and marker D12S1701 (47.7 Mb).

Zimprich et al. (2004) concluded that the PARK8 locus causes disease in a subset of white families with autosomal dominant parkinsonism, with an estimated 0.32 proportion of linked families. They suggested that PARK8 could be a more common locus.

Wszolek et al. (2004) reported follow-up of a parkinsonian kindred first described in 1995. Since that report, 4 more individuals had become affected, with a mean age at onset of 65 years. All 4 had the cardinal signs of Parkinson disease and responded well to levodopa.

Wszolek et al. (2004) reported 4 autopsies in the kindred. All 4 showed neuronal loss and gliosis in the substantia nigra, but the other pathology varied. One case had Lewy bodies limited to brainstem nuclei and a second had diffuse Lewy bodies. A third had neurofibrillary tangles without Lewy bodies, and the fourth had neither neurofibrillary tangles nor Lewy bodies.
In this autosomal dominant parkinsonism kindred, Wszolek et al. (2004) reported that genetic studies suggested linkage to the PARK8 locus on chromosome 12.
Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2004) cloned a novel gene in the PARK8 region and found missense mutations in it that segregated with PARK8-linked Parkinson disease in 5 families from England and Spain.

Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2004) named the protein encoded by the PARK8 gene 'dardarin', from the Basque word 'dardara', meaning tremor. They chose this name because of the tremor seen in Parkinson disease and because several of the families were of Basque descent.
Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2004) noted that PARK8, identified by Funayama and colleagues in 2002, appears to be a common cause of familial Parkinson disease.

Zimprich et al. (2004) used high-resolution recombination mapping and candidate gene sequencing in 46 families with autosomal dominant, late-onset parkinsonism previously linked to chromosome 12p11.2-q13.1 (PARK8) and found 6 disease-segregating mutations (5 missense and 1 putative splice site mutation) in the LRRK2 gene.

Zimprich et al. (2004) noted that they had previously linked families with autosomal dominant, late-onset parkinsonism to chromosome 12p11.2-q13.1 (PARK8), and refined the region by high-resolution recombination mapping.

Zimprich et al. (2004) reported 6 postmortem examinations of affected mutation carriers from families A and D that showed brainstem dopaminergic degeneration accompanied by strikingly diverse pathologies, including Lewy body Parkinson disease, diffuse Lewy body disease, nigral degeneration without distinctive histopathology, and progressive supranuclear palsy-like pathology. Clinical diagnoses of parkinsonism with dementia, amyotrophy, or both were also noted.

Zimprich et al. (2004) noted that LRRK2 belongs to the ROCO protein family, containing a MAPKKK-class protein kinase domain and several other major functional domains, and suggested that LRRK2 may be central to the pathogenesis of several major neurodegenerative disorders associated with parkinsonism.

Nichols et al. (2005) screened genomic DNA from 767 affected individuals in 358 multiplex families with familial Parkinson disease, plus controls, for the LRRK2 gly2019-to-ser (G2019S) mutation. Thirty-five affected individuals (5%) carried the mutation: 34 were heterozygous and 1 was homozygous. The authors suggested that this single LRRK2 mutation causes Parkinson disease in 5% of individuals with familial disease.
Nichols et al. (2005) reported that individuals carrying the LRRK2 G2019S mutation had clinical findings typical of idiopathic Parkinson disease.
Nichols et al. (2005) recommended that screening for the LRRK2 G2019S mutation be part of genetic testing for Parkinson disease.

Di Fonzo et al. (2005) sequenced the coding region of LRRK2 in 61 unrelated families with Parkinson disease and autosomal dominant inheritance. They found a heterozygous gly2019-to-ser (G2019S) mutation in 4 of the 61 families (6.6%). The families came from Italy, Portugal, and Brazil, which showed that the mutation occurs in different populations.
Di Fonzo et al. (2005) reported that the phenotype associated with the LRRK2 G2019S mutation was broad and included both early and late disease onset.

Di Fonzo et al. (2005) concluded that LRRK2 G2019S is a common mutation associated with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease. It was present in 6.6% of the unrelated autosomal dominant families they studied.

Gilks et al. (2005) directly sequenced exon 41 of the LRRK2 gene in 482 patients with idiopathic Parkinson disease, 263 of whom had pathologically confirmed disease. They found the heterozygous 2877510G-A mutation, which causes a gly2019-to-ser (G2019S) substitution, in 8 (1.6%) of the patients. The authors concluded that a common single Mendelian mutation is implicated in sporadic Parkinson disease.
Gilks et al. (2005) suggested that testing for the LRRK2 G2019S mutation will be important in the management and genetic counseling of patients with Parkinson disease.

Paisàn-Ruìz et al. (2005) genetically characterized four Basque families with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease and found evidence for linkage to the PARK8 locus, with a maximum 2-point lod score of 3.21 (theta = 0.00) at marker D12S345.

Paisàn-Ruìz et al. (2005) reported that affected members of four Basque families with PARK8-linked autosomal dominant Parkinson disease had the clinical features of typical PD, including rigidity, akinesia, and a good response to levodopa therapy. Mean age at disease onset was 55 years.

Funayama et al. (2005) found a missense mutation in the kinase domain of the LRRK2 gene in affected members of the Japanese Sagamihara family with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease. This family was the basis for the original definition of the PARK8 locus.

nodes.label: Funayama et al. (2005) noted that the pathology in the Sagamihara family was distinctive, with pure nigral degeneration and no Lewy bodies.
Funayama et al. (2005) did not find the Sagamihara family mutation, or other known LRRK2 mutations, in Japanese patients with sporadic Parkinson disease.

Lesage et al. (2005) performed LRRK2 haplotype analyses in European and North African families with Parkinson disease. They concluded that the G2019S mutation arose from a common founder dating from the 13th century.

Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) sequenced all 51 LRRK2 coding exons in 23 probands from families with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease and found heterozygous LRRK2 mutations in 3 of them. Two probands carried the known G2019S substitution. Mutation frequencies were checked in 180 neurologically normal controls. In a large family, G2019S segregated completely with PD.
Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) found a novel heterozygous I1371V substitution in LRRK2 in 1 of 23 probands from families with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease.

Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) reported that the disease in the 3 families with LRRK2 mutations had a phenotype indistinguishable from typical Parkinson disease. Age at onset was very variable in all 3 families, and APOE genotypes did not explain this variation.

In a case-control study, Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2005) genotyped 4 coding LRRK2 polymorphisms in 121 patients with PD and 250 normal controls, mostly white Canadians. In the patient group, 84% had onset before age 50 and 42% had a positive family history. None of the polymorphisms was associated with PD at the allelic or genotypic level (p > 0.17). Neither these genotypes nor APOE genotypes modified age at onset (p > 0.20).

Farrer et al. (2005) screened 786 Parkinson disease probands, 32 affected siblings, 1,044 unaffected siblings, and 278 unrelated controls for 9 LRRK2 mutations using allelic discrimination assays. Mutations were identified in 6 probands with PD, 1 affected sibling, 1 unaffected sibling, and 1 unrelated control. The authors concluded that LRRK2 mutations only rarely cause idiopathic PD.

Skipper et al. (2005) used tagging SNPs to evaluate common genetic variation across LRRK2 in a large, epidemiologically matched case-control series of 932 Chinese individuals with sporadic Parkinson disease or controls. Both single-tSNP and haplotype analyses gave significant evidence of disease association. Carrying 2 copies of one haplotype sharply increased disease risk (OR = 5.5, 95% CI 2.1-14.0, P = 0.0001). The authors concluded that common variation within LRRK2 contributes to the risk of sporadic Parkinson disease in the Chinese population.

Ross et al. (2006) found the LRRK2 G2019S substitution in about 2% (8) of 405 Parkinson disease/Lewy body disease cases. They also found it in 1 control subject and 1 patient with Alzheimer disease, and attributed this to reduced penetrance.
Ross et al. (2006) reported that Lewy body disease was the most common neuropathology in Parkinson disease associated with LRRK2 G2019S.

Giasson et al. (2006) identified 3 autopsied patients with the LRRK2 G2019S mutation. Two had classic Parkinson disease with Lewy bodies, one of whom also had concurrent pathologic changes consistent with Alzheimer disease. The third had parkinsonism without Lewy bodies but showed dystrophic neurites in the substantia nigra intensely stained for Lrrk2; such Lrrk2 accumulations were unique to this patient.

Using a Lrrk2-specific antibody, Giasson et al. (2006) found that Lrrk2 was not detected in other types of pathologic inclusions, and that Lrrk2 is predominantly a soluble approximately 250-kD cytoplasmic protein expressed throughout the brain and in many other organs. They suggested that LRRK2 mutations may prime select neuronal populations to cellular insults that can lead to aberrant protein aggregation.
Zhu et al. (2006) reported that LRRK2 protein is a component of Lewy bodies.

Ishihara et al. (2006) described 29 patients with familial Parkinson disease who were homozygous for the LRRK2 6055G>A (G2019S) mutation. The patients came from an international consortium and included 23 Tunisians, 2 Algerians, 2 US patients, 1 Canadian, and 1 Moroccan. The authors saw no observable differences between the homozygous phenotype and previously published descriptions of heterozygous patients. They concluded that LRRK2-related PD has typical clinical features and that these similarities do not support a gene dosage effect.

Rajput et al. (2006) described a family (Family SK) with slowly progressive parkinsonism. The affected proband had tau-immunopositive neurofibrillary tangle pathology, not the alpha-synuclein-immunopositive Lewy body pathology mainly linked to LRRK2 G2019S.

In Family SK, Rajput et al. (2006) found that the LRRK2 G2019S variant segregated with slowly progressive parkinsonism. The authors suggested that alpha-synucleinopathy and tauopathy may be alternate outcomes of the same underlying genetic cause.
Rajput et al. (2006) found no evidence that either tau or alpha-synuclein protein interacts directly with LRRK2.

Orr-Urtreger et al. (2007) screened Jewish Israeli patients with Parkinson disease for the LRRK2 G2019S, I2012T, I2020T, and R1441G/C/H mutations. Only G2019S was found. It was present in 14.8% of Ashkenazi and 2.7% of non-Ashkenazi patients, and in 26% of Ashkenazi familial cases and 10.6% of Ashkenazi apparently sporadic cases. Carrier frequencies in Ashkenazi and non-Ashkenazi controls were 2.4% and 0.4%, respectively.

Orr-Urtreger et al. (2007) used 6 microsatellite markers spanning the LRRK2 gene to determine haplotypes in 76 G2019S carriers and 50 Ashkenazi noncarrier patients with Parkinson disease. A common shared haplotype was found in all non-Ashkenazi and half-Ashkenazi carriers, and in all full-Ashkenazi carriers tested except two.

Orr-Urtreger et al. (2007) found that women and patients with a positive family history of Parkinson disease were significantly overrepresented among LRRK2 G2019S carriers. Age at onset was similar in carriers and noncarriers. The authors concluded that sex affects the frequency of the mutation among patients.

Chen-Plotkin et al. (2008) screened 434 individuals for the common LRRK2 G2019S mutation and several other previously reported LRRK2 mutations. The group was made up of 254 patients from neurodegenerative disease clinics and 180 neurodegenerative disease autopsy cases from the University of Pennsylvania brain bank. Eight cases carried a LRRK2 mutation.

Chen-Plotkin et al. (2008) found that 2 of the 8 LRRK2 mutation carriers first showed cognitive deficits and were clinically diagnosed with corticobasal syndrome and primary progressive aphasia, respectively. The authors concluded that LRRK2-associated neurodegenerative disease may be more clinically varied than previously assumed.

Liu et al. (2008) used the GAL4/UAS system to make transgenic Drosophila expressing either wildtype human LRRK2 or LRRK2 G2019S, the most common PD-associated mutation. Expressing either form in photoreceptor cells caused retinal degeneration. Expressing either form in neurons caused adult-onset selective loss of dopaminergic neurons, locomotor dysfunction, and early death. G2019S-LRRK2 caused a more severe parkinsonism-like phenotype than equivalent levels of wildtype LRRK2.

In the Drosophila model of Liu et al. (2008), L-DOPA treatment improved the locomotor impairment caused by mutant LRRK2 but did not prevent loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons. The authors described this as, to their knowledge, the first in vivo gain-of-function model that recapitulates several key features of LRRK2-linked human parkinsonism.

Choi et al. (2008) sequenced SNCA, PARKIN, DJ-1, PINK1, and LRRK2 and analyzed gene dosage by MLPA in 72 unrelated Korean patients with early-onset Parkinson disease (onset at or before age 50) from ten movement disorder clinics in South Korea. Nine patients (12.5%) were heterozygous for the LRRK2 G2385R variant, a known Asian susceptibility allele, and none carried the G2019S mutation.

Choi et al. (2008) found that the LRRK2 G2019S mutation was absent among 72 Korean early-onset PD patients, whereas the G2385R risk variant was present heterozygously in 12.5%. Overall, variants in PARKIN, PINK1, LRRK2, and SNCA accounted for causes or genetic risk factors in 25% of Korean early-onset PD, with PARKIN mutations the most common genetic cause.

Silveira-Moriyama et al. (2008) used the University of Pennsylvania Smell Test (UPSIT) to evaluate olfaction in 19 parkinsonian and 2 asymptomatic carriers of the LRRK2 G2019S mutation. The mean UPSIT score in parkinsonian carriers was lower than in healthy controls (p less than 0.001) and similar to that of patients with Parkinson disease (p greater than 0.999), whereas the 2 asymptomatic carriers had smell test results in the normal range.

Silveira-Moriyama et al. (2008) performed postmortem examination of the rhinencephalon in 4 parkinsonian carriers of the LRRK2 G2019S mutation, including 1 patient clinically found to have hyposmia, and found alpha-synuclein deposition with Lewy bodies in the olfactory pathways in all cases.
Lesage et al. (2008) asked whether the common LRRK2 G2019S mutation is related to dyskinesias in North African patients with Parkinson disease.

Nandhagopal et al. (2008) performed multitracer PET of presynaptic dopaminergic integrity in 13 members of family D (Western Nebraska), a parkinsonian kindred carrying the LRRK2 R1441C mutation. Five subjects were rescanned 2 to 3 years later. In 2 mutation carriers and 1 genealogically at-risk subject, PET markers declined significantly faster than the expected rate in healthy controls. The authors concluded that presymptomatic members of the kindred had dopaminergic dysfunction that progressed over time.

In the LRRK2 R1441C family D, Nandhagopal et al. (2008) found that reduced dopamine transporter binding was the earliest sign of subclinical dopaminergic dysfunction. Progression to clinical disease was generally associated with the emergence of abnormal fluorodopa uptake.

Lesage et al. (2009) sequenced all 51 coding exons of LRRK2 in index cases from 226 Parkinson disease families compatible with autosomal dominant inheritance, mostly from France (182) and North Africa (14). They found 79 sequence variants, 29 of them novel. Eight potentially or proven pathogenic mutations were found in 22 probands (9.7%), and most were located in the functional domains of the LRRK2 protein. The authors concluded that LRRK2 mutations are a common cause of autosomal dominant PD in Europe and North Africa.

Lesage et al. (2009) identified the common LRRK2 G2019S mutation in 13 of 226 probands (5.8%) with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease. Six of these probands were from North Africa, which was 43% of the North African probands.

Lesage et al. (2009) found 4 novel LRRK2 amino acid substitutions that they considered potentially pathogenic (S52F, N363S, I810V, and R1325Q) in probands with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease. They also found 2 novel variants, H1216R and T1410M, that they considered probably not causative.
Lesage et al. (2009) found the known heterozygous LRRK2 mutations R1441H and I1371V in 2 probands each with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease. They found the E334K variant in a single patient.

In a genome-wide association study and two replication studies involving a total of 2,011 PD cases and 18,381 controls from Japan, Satake et al. (2009) detected strong association of Parkinson disease with variants at LRRK2 on 12q12 (P = 2.72 x 10(-8)), as well as at SNCA on 4q22 (P = 7.35 x 10(-17)), both loci implicated in autosomal dominant parkinsonism. Comparison with a GWAS of individuals of European ancestry identified LRRK2 as a risk locus shared between populations; the authors concluded that autosomal dominant parkinsonism loci are involved in typical PD.

Satake et al. (2009) identified PARK16 on 1q32 and BST1 on 4p15 as new PD susceptibility loci in a Japanese GWAS, and found BST1 and MAPT to show population differences compared with a European GWAS, suggesting that population differences contribute to genetic heterogeneity in PD.

Alcalay et al. (2009) genotyped 925 probands with early-onset Parkinson disease (age at onset 50 years or younger) from 13 movement disorders centers for the LRRK2 mutations G2019S, I2020T, R1441C, and Y1699C. Thirty-four probands (3.7%), 14 of whom had been reported before, carried G2019S, and one Ashkenazi Jewish carrier was homozygous. No other mutations were found. Carriers were more likely to be Ashkenazi Jewish than non-carriers (55.9% vs 11.9%) but were not more likely to have a first-degree relative with PD.

Alcalay et al. (2009) found that G2019S carriers with early-onset PD had a lower UPDRS tremor score than non-carriers (P = 0.03) and were more likely to have the postural instability and gait difficulty (PIGD) motor phenotype (92.3% vs 58.9%). Only 3.8% of carriers had the tremor-dominant phenotype, compared with 27.4% of non-carriers. The association with PIGD remained after adjustment for disease duration and Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry (OR 17.7) and held in Ashkenazi and non-Ashkenazi probands analyzed separately. The authors found this contrasted with earlier reports linking LRRK2 to tremor-dominant disease.

Alcalay et al. (2009) found that G2019S carriers and non-carriers with early-onset PD were similar in age at onset (range 13 to 50 years), disease duration, age at examination, UPDRS-III score, MMSE score, and levodopa dose. Among carriers with complete UPDRS data, 88.5% had asymmetric onset and 44.0% presented with rest tremor. Although PIGD was associated with more severe disease than the tremor-dominant phenotype in the whole cohort, carriers and non-carriers did not differ on these measures of severity.

Gan-Or et al. (2010) screened 600 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with Parkinson disease for the LRRK2 G2019S mutation and 8 GBA mutations. They compared the initial symptoms the patients reported across 3 groups: GBA mutation carriers, LRRK2 G2019S carriers, and non-carriers. More LRRK2 G2019S carriers reported muscle stiffness (rigidity, p = 0.007) and balance disturbances (p = 0.008) as initial symptoms. More GBA mutation carriers reported slowness (bradykinesia, p = 0.021). The authors suggested that LRRK2 and GBA mutations have distinct effects on the initial presentation of PD.

Dächsel and Farrer (2010) reviewed the molecular genetics and functional biology of LRRK2 in parkinsonism. They noted that genetic mutations that predispose to PD are diagnostically useful in early or atypical presentations. They also noted that affected and asymptomatic LRRK2 carriers provide an opportunity to define the natural history of PD, including penetrance, motor symptoms, nonmotor comorbidities and associated biomarkers.

Using an in vivo EGFP reporter carrying let-7-binding sites in its 3'UTR, Gehrke et al. (2010) showed that ubiquitous (Da-Gal4) or dopaminergic neuron-specific (TH-Gal4) expression of pathogenic Drosophila dLRRK(I1915T) or human LRRK2(G2019S) stimulated reporter expression more than the wild-type proteins, whereas dLRRK RNAi decreased reporter expression and the kinase-dead dLRRK(3KD) had no effect; gfp mRNA levels were unchanged, leading the authors to conclude that LRRK2 antagonizes let-7 function at the translational level in a kinase-dependent manner.

In HEK293T cells transfected with a luciferase reporter bearing let-7-binding sites in the 3'UTR, Gehrke et al. (2010) found that hLRRK2(I2020T) or hLRRK2(G2019S) efficiently suppressed the inhibitory effect of let-7 on reporter expression, and that introduction of kinase-inactivating (3KD) mutations into these proteins abolished the effect, supporting kinase activity-dependency of pathogenic LRRK2 action.

Gehrke et al. (2010) reported that mutant hLRRK2 carrying the pathogenic R1441G mutation had no effect on let-7 miRNA function and that transgenic flies expressing dLRRK carrying the equivalent R1069G mutation showed no dopaminergic neuron loss, suggesting that this mutation acts through a different mechanism from G2019S and I2020T.

Gehrke et al. (2010) showed by co-immunoprecipitation that LRRK2 physically associates with Argonaute proteins of the RNA-induced silencing complex: transfected hLRRK2 associated with hAgo2 in HEK293T cells, transgenic hLRRK2 associated with dAgo1 in fly head extracts, and endogenous hLRRK2 or dLRRK associated with hAgo2 or dAgo1, respectively; because similar results were obtained with or without RNase A treatment, the authors concluded the interaction was likely direct and not RNA-mediated. let-7 levels were not changed in hLRRK2(G2019S) or dLRRK(I1915T) transgenics.

In Drosophila, Gehrke et al. (2010) found that dAgo1 protein was significantly reduced by pathogenic hLRRK2 in aged flies (but not young flies) and increased in dLRRK mutants, and that ago1 heterozygosity exacerbated the climbing defect and dopaminergic neuron loss phenotypes of pathogenic dLRRK or hLRRK2 transgenics, while aged ago1 heterozygotes alone (with ~26% reduction of dAgo1) showed no obvious phenotype.

Gehrke et al. (2010) demonstrated a genetic interaction between LRRK2 and the miRNA-processing enzyme Dicer in Drosophila: in a TH-Gal4>dLRRK(I1915T) background, Dicer1 overexpression suppressed and Dicer1 RNAi exacerbated dLRRK(I1915T) toxicity, whereas stronger Dicer1 inhibition in a dicer1 heterozygous background itself caused dopaminergic neuron loss and climbing defects that were partially reduced by dLRRK RNAi.

Gehrke et al. (2010) found that 4E-BP1 associated with hAgo2 in HEK293T cells and that dLRRK(I1915T) and hLRRK2(G2019S) promoted this interaction more effectively than wild-type proteins, presumably through increased phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 and preferential binding of phospho-4E-BP1 to hAgo2; phospho-mimetic 4E-BP(TE) attenuated let-7 effects and was toxic to dopaminergic neurons, whereas non-phosphorylatable 4E-BP(TA) blocked the ability of hLRRK2(G2019S) to antagonize let-7. The authors concluded that pathogenic hLRRK2 with hyperactive kinase activity promotes association of phospho-4E-BP with hAgo2, relieving miRNA-mediated translational repression.

By mRNA translational profiling of Da-Gal4>dLRRK(WT) versus Da-Gal4>dLRRK(I1915T) fly heads, Gehrke et al. (2010) identified e2f1 and dp as targets whose translation is upregulated by pathogenic LRRK2; E2F1 and DP protein were increased by dLRRK(I1915T) or hLRRK2(G2019S) and decreased in dLRRK(-/-) mutants without changes in mRNA level, and removing one copy of e2f1 or dp, or overexpressing the negative regulator RBF, suppressed the dopaminergic neuron phenotypes and oxidative stress sensitivity of dLRRK(I1915T) animals, whereas removing one copy of lkb1 had no effect.

Gehrke et al. (2010) identified a functional miR-184*-binding site in the Drosophila e2f1 3'UTR and a functional let-7-binding site in the dp 3'UTR by reporter assays, with mutation of two central seed nucleotides abolishing the miRNA effect; co-transfection of pathogenic hLRRK2 strongly relieved the repressive effects of let-7 and miR-184* on the dp- and e2f1-3'UTR reporters, respectively.

Gehrke et al. (2010) showed that overexpression of pre-let-7 or injection of synthetic let-7 into wild-type fly heads reduced DP protein, and pre-miR-184* or miR-184* injection reduced E2F1, validating E2F1 and DP as in vivo miRNA targets; dopaminergic-neuron-specific pre-let-7 or pre-miR-184* overexpression or mature miRNA injection partially rescued TH-Gal4>dLRRK(I1915T) phenotypes, whereas buffer or control miR-10 injection had no effect, indicating that miRNA regulation of E2F1 and DP is causally involved in dLRRK(I1915T) pathogenesis.

Gehrke et al. (2010) showed that loss of miRNA function phenocopied pathogenic LRRK2 in Drosophila: homozygous let-7 mutants (Delta-let-7) had reduced locomotor activity, specific reduction of dopaminergic neurons rescuable by a let-7 transgene, and increased DP level, with phenotypes suppressed by removing one copy of dp or e2f1; injection of anti-let-7fS or anti-miR-184*fS antagomirs into wild-type flies increased DP or E2F1 levels and caused specific dopaminergic neuron loss and reduced climbing activity, effects attenuated by e2f1/+ or dp/+ heterozygosity, and E2F1 overexpression alone was sufficient to cause dopaminergic neuron degeneration.

To prove the specificity of the let-7/dp mRNA interaction in dopaminergic neurons, Gehrke et al. (2010) generated flies expressing a dp target protector (dp-TPlet-7), whose ubiquitous expression caused DP overproduction without affecting dp mRNA level and whose TH-Gal4-driven expression led to dopaminergic neuron loss and reduced climbing activity, and genomic dp transgenes with non-functional let-7-binding sites (gDPmut), which caused DP accumulation and, although rescuing viability of Df/dpR217H transheterozygotes, produced loss of dopaminergic neurons and locomotor defects.

Gehrke et al. (2010) concluded that gain-of-function LRRK2 mutations cause Parkinson disease by impairing the miRNA pathway: pathogenic LRRK2 antagonizes let-7 and miR-184*, leading to overproduction of E2F1/DP, whose upregulation in post-mitotic neurons may lead to abortive cell division and cell death; because LRRK2 effects manifested only in aged animals, the authors suggested LRRK2 is particularly important for miRNA regulation under stress conditions and proposed novel miRNA-based therapeutic strategies.

Gehrke et al. (2010) noted that GMR-Gal4-driven dLRRK(I1915T) expression in the eye did not affect the activities of the bantam and miR-14 miRNAs, suggesting that pathogenic dLRRK may regulate miRNA function in a miRNA- and/or tissue-specific manner.

Gehrke et al. (2010) stated that gain-of-function mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) cause familial as well as sporadic Parkinson disease characterized by age-dependent degeneration of dopaminergic neurons, and that the molecular mechanism of LRRK2 action was not known.

Tan et al. (2010) analyzed 13 SNPs at Parkinson disease GWAS-linked loci (PARK16, PARK8, PARK1, and BST1) in 2 case-control cohorts totaling 1,349 ethnic Chinese subjects. PARK8 SNPs were associated with an increased risk of PD. A pooled analysis with 2 Japanese replication cohorts, involving 1,366 PD patients and 16,669 controls, showed robust association with the PARK8 locus. The authors concluded that the strength of association was similar in Chinese and Japanese subjects.

Lee et al. (2010) screened 84 kinase and phosphatase inhibitors at 16 microM against LRRK2 autophosphorylation and LRRK2-mediated phosphorylation of myelin basic protein, and identified 8 compounds, including indolinone compounds (staurosporine, GF 109203X, Ro 31-8220, 5-iodotubercidin, GW5074, indirubin-3-prime-monooxime) and anthracene compounds (SP 600125, damnacanthal), that substantially inhibited LRRK2 kinase activity; none of the inhibitors enhanced LRRK2 kinase activity.

Lee et al. (2010) determined IC50 values of the 8 inhibitors against autophosphorylation and MBP phosphorylation by wildtype and G2019S LRRK2, and found that all inhibitors except indirubin-3-prime-monooxime had relatively similar potency against wildtype and G2019S LRRK2 autophosphorylation; indirubin-3-prime-monooxime more potently inhibited LRRK2 G2019S autophosphorylation. All 8 inhibitors had a similar inhibitory profile against LRRK1.

Because LRRK2 and LRRK1 are related to the MAP kinase kinase kinase Raf, Lee et al. (2010) tested additional Raf kinase inhibitors and concluded that GW5074 inhibited both LRRK2 and LRRK1 kinase activities, that sorafenib and Raf inhibitor IV were relatively selective for LRRK2 kinase activity, and that ZM336372 had minimal to no effect on either kinase. GW5074 and indirubin-3-prime-monooxime, but not ZM336372 or indirubin, also inhibited LRRK2-mediated phosphorylation of 4E-BP1, a putative physiologic LRRK2 substrate.

Lee et al. (2010) found that overexpression of both wildtype and G2019S LRRK2 led to primary cortical neuron injury assessed by neurite shortening, and that LRRK2 G2019S overexpression also led to cell death assessed by TUNEL, whereas kinase-dead versions of LRRK2 wildtype (D1994A) and LRRK2 G2019S (G2019S, D1994A) were devoid of toxicity.

Lee et al. (2010) showed that treatment of cortical cultures with GW5074, indirubin-3-prime-monooxime, or the relatively LRRK2-selective inhibitor sorafenib (each 0.5 microM) attenuated or completely prevented LRRK2 G2019S cell injury and cell death, whereas ZM336372 and indirubin, which do not inhibit LRRK2 or LRRK1 kinase activity, failed to protect; the authors concluded that the protection was due to inhibition of LRRK2 kinase activity rather than inhibition of Raf, cyclin-dependent kinase, or GSK3-beta.

Lee et al. (2010) developed a herpes simplex virus amplicon-based mouse model of LRRK2 dopaminergic neurotoxicity. HSV amplicon-mediated delivery of LRRK2 G2019S induced significant loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive substantia nigra neurons 3 weeks after stereotaxic injection into the ipsilateral striatum compared with LRRK2 wildtype and eGFP control viruses, whereas the kinase-dead LRRK2 G2019S, D1994A caused no neuronal loss, despite equivalent levels of overexpression.

Lee et al. (2010) reported that twice daily intraperitoneal injections of the LRRK2 kinase inhibitors GW5074 and indirubin-3-prime-monooxime (2.5 mg/kg) attenuated the loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons induced by HSV-LRRK2 G2019S in mice compared with DMSO- and indirubin-injected controls, and that GW5074 also rescued the reduced density of TH-positive fibers and prevented the increase in isolectin B4-positive inflammatory cells in the striatum and substantia nigra compacta.

Lee et al. (2010) concluded that their identification of kinase inhibitors that inhibit LRRK2 kinase activity and protect against LRRK2 toxicity in vitro and in vivo established that LRRK2-induced degeneration of neurons in vivo is kinase dependent and that pharmacologic LRRK2 kinase inhibition is a potentially promising neuroprotective therapeutic modality for Parkinson disease; they cautioned, however, that an authentic LRRK2 substrate has yet to be identified, raising concerns about the physiologic relevance of screens based on autophosphorylation and artificial substrates.

Lee et al. (2010) noted that LRRK2 mutations are a common cause of Parkinson disease, that patients with LRRK2 mutations are clinically and neurochemically indistinguishable from those with idiopathic Parkinson disease, and that disease-segregating LRRK2 mutations lead to neurotoxicity in vitro and loss of dopamine neurons in patients with Parkinson disease.

Alcalay et al. (2010) screened 953 patients with early-onset Parkinson disease (age at onset 50 years or younger) from 13 movement disorders centers in the CORE-PD study. Patients were recruited without regard to family history. Of these, 35 (3.6%) carried the LRRK2 G2019S mutation. Among the 31 G2019S carriers with no mutation in another gene, 30 were heterozygous and 1 was homozygous. One additional patient carried the LRRK2 G2385R variant, and no other pathogenic LRRK2 mutations (R1441C, I2020T, Y1699C) were found.

Alcalay et al. (2010) reported that LRRK2 G2019S carriers were more likely to have Jewish ancestry: 55% of G2019S-only carriers were Jewish, compared with 12% of noncarriers. Among patients with Jewish ancestry, 13.6% of those with a family history of PD and 12.2% of those without one carried G2019S. Grandparents' country of origin was known for 11 of the 15 non-Jewish G2019S carriers: 4 reported Southern European descent (Italy or Portugal), 4 mixed European descent, 1 Eastern European ancestry, and 2 Puerto Rican ancestry.

Alcalay et al. (2010) found that LRRK2 G2019S carriers with early-onset PD were more likely to have the postural instability and gait difficulty (PIGD) motor phenotype than noncarriers: 96% (25 carriers) versus 58% of noncarriers. Carriers had a mean age at onset of 42 years, similar to noncarriers. The presenting symptom did not differ significantly between mutation groups.

Alcalay et al. (2010) found that PRKN carriers were more likely than LRRK2 carriers to report a family history of PD, even though LRRK2-related PD is autosomal dominant. Among G2019S carriers, 3.6% of patients with a family history of PD carried the mutation, compared with 3.1% of those without one. The authors suggested that one explanation was incomplete penetrance of G2019S. They also noted that the penetrance of these mutations remains unknown.

Alcalay et al. (2010) identified 4 patients who carried LRRK2 G2019S together with a mutation in another gene. One Jewish man carried a heterozygous PRKN exon 5-6 deletion (onset at age 41). One non-Jewish man carried GBA L444P (onset at age 31). Two Jewish patients carried GBA N370S (onset at ages 47 and 49). None of these patients reported PD in a first-degree relative.

Saunders-Pullman et al. (2011) gave the University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT) to 31 patients with Parkinson disease related to the LRRK2 G2019S mutation (manifesting carriers), 30 patients with PD who did not carry the mutation, 28 mutation-carrier family members without PD (nonmanifesting carriers), and 46 controls. Compared with controls, mean scores were lower in nonmanifesting carriers (difference = -3.518, p = 0.006), manifesting carriers (difference = -7.677) and noncarrier PD patients (difference = -13.810). Olfaction was better in LRRK2 manifesting carriers than in non-LRRK2 PD patients (difference = 6.13, p = 0.0012). The authors concluded that olfaction is impaired in G2019S-related PD, but less overall than in other PD.

Saunders-Pullman et al. (2011) found that olfaction was impaired in a subset of 28 nonmanifesting LRRK2 G2019S carriers who did not have PD. The authors suggested that olfaction may be a marker for the development of PD in this group and that longitudinal studies are warranted.

Marras et al. (2011) used a family study design to compare 25 individuals with LRRK2 G2019S-associated Parkinson disease with 84 individuals with idiopathic PD, recruited from 4 movement disorders centers. Tremor was more often a presenting feature in LRRK2-PD. LRRK2-PD patients also had better olfactory identification, higher Beck Depression Inventory scores, and worse color discrimination on the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-Hue test. The authors concluded that the phenotype was largely overlapping with idiopathic PD.

Marras et al. (2011) found that postural or action tremor was more common in 29 nonmanifesting LRRK2 G2019S carriers than in 53 noncarriers from the same families. They suggested that postural or action tremor may be an early sign. Nonparkinsonian family members had higher UPDRS motor scores, more constipation, and worse color discrimination than controls, whether or not they carried the mutation.

Aasly et al. (2012) measured CSF amyloid beta-42 (Abeta42), total tau, and phosphorylated tau in 26 LRRK2 mutation carriers, 18 asymptomatic and 8 with a phenotype resembling sporadic Parkinson disease. They compared these levels with PET measures of striatal dopaminergic function using 18F-6-fluoro-L-dopa (FD), 11C-dihydrotetrabenazine, and 11C-d-threo-methylphenidate. Lower CSF Abeta42 and tau levels correlated with lower striatal dopaminergic function on all 3 tracers, and the association between Abeta42 and FD uptake was significant. When the analysis was limited to carriers of G2019S, the most common LRRK2 variant in the cohort, the correlations with tau were also significant.
Decreased amyloid beta 42 peptide CSF concentration

Aasly et al. (2012) concluded that how amyloid beta and tau are handled is likely important in both LRRK2-related and sporadic Parkinson disease, even in early phases of the disease. They suggested that these CSF proteins might be useful as biomarkers of early or presymptomatic disease.

Inzelberg et al. (2012) genotyped 490 Jewish patients with Parkinson disease for the LRRK2 G2019S mutation and found 79 carriers (16.1%). Non-skin cancer was more common in carriers than in noncarriers (18 of 79 carriers, 23%, vs 49 noncarriers, 12%; p = 0.01, OR 2.18, 95% CI 1.19-3.99). Among Ashkenazi patients, the age-adjusted OR for carriers was 3.38 (95% CI 1.64-6.97, p = 0.0009). The authors concluded that Ashkenazi Jewish patients with PD who carry G2019S are more likely to have a concomitant non-skin cancer than noncarriers.
Bandmann and Cookson (2012) discussed whether the link between LRRK2-associated Parkinson disease and cancer is causal or only an association.

Koch et al. (2026) noted that gain of function of LRRK2 increases Parkinson disease risk. They stated that heterozygous predicted loss-of-function (pLoF) variants of LRRK2 have not been associated with any phenotype, including Parkinson disease. They reported this while assessing the safety of chronic LRRK2 inhibition in the Pakistan Genome Resource (173,303 exomes and genomes).

In the Pakistan Genome Resource, Koch et al. (2026) found a 42-year-old individual homozygous for an LRRK2 splice donor variant (c.706+1G>T). This person had a low eGFR of 68 ml/min, consistent with early-stage kidney disease. In this person's exome, the authors found no damaging missense or high-confidence pLoF variants in known kidney disease genes.

Koch et al. (2026) found a 25-year-old individual in the Pakistan Genome Resource homozygous for an LRRK2 frameshift variant (Arg1639GlyfsTer15). This person had chronic kidney disease, with an eGFR of 14 ml/min.

In a recall-by-genotype study, Koch et al. (2026) identified a 49-year-old woman homozygous for an LRRK2 splice donor variant (c.1418+1G>T), confirmed by Sanger sequencing. She was the only homozygous carrier in her family. Her eGFR was 51 ml/min, suggestive of kidney disease, and lower than that of all 13 recruited relatives: 6 heterozygous carriers and 7 non-carriers.

Koch et al. (2026) said their sample of human LRRK2 homozygous loss-of-function carriers was small. They concluded that the kidney dysfunction seen in these carriers supports the adverse renal phenotypes reported in LRRK2-knockout rodents and in preclinical studies of LRRK2 inhibitors in rats and non-human primates. They suggested that kidney function be monitored during long-term LRRK2 inhibition.
